teaser: She posed in a bathtub all winter. The riverbank had been waiting since summer.
review_notes:
Elizabeth Siddal's age when posing (born July 1829, posed winter 1851-52): given as twenty-two.
Bath heated by oil lamps that went out; Siddal's father threatening legal action and Millais paying the doctor's bills (often quoted as a demand of 50 pounds, settled lower).
Landscape painted by the Hogsmill River at Ewell, Surrey, from July 1851: up to eleven hours a day, six days a week, about five months.
Millais's letter about the flies of Surrey, the wind and the threatened summons for trespassing and destroying hay: paraphrased from his letters.
Water vole painted then removed after relatives failed to identify it (hare, rabbit, dog, cat).
Dress bought secondhand for four pounds, “all flowered over in silver embroidery” (Millais's letter).
Flower meanings (poppy, violets, pansies, dog roses, willow, forget-me-nots, loosestrife as “long purples”): follow Tate's commentary. The species of the purple flowers on the skirt (spot at x 0.645, y 0.735) should be checked on the zoom image: read here as pansies.
“Bonny sweet Robin” line sung by Ophelia in Hamlet, act 4.
Siddal died in 1862 aged thirty-two from a laudanum overdose.
Given to the nation by Henry Tate in 1894.

lesson.text: London, the winter of 1852. A young woman lies fully dressed in a bathtub of water, hour after hour, playing dead. Oil lamps under the tub are supposed to keep the water warm. One day they go out. The painter, lost in his work, does not notice. She says nothing and stays in the cold.

Her name was Elizabeth Siddal, and she was twenty-two. She came down with a severe cold. Her father threatened the painter, John Everett Millais, with legal action until he agreed to pay the doctor's bills. By then Millais had what he wanted: the face and hands of a drowning girl.

The girl is Ophelia, from Shakespeare's “Hamlet”. Hamlet, the man she loves, has killed her father, and grief has broken her mind. Hanging garlands on a willow, she falls into a stream. Her dress spreads and holds her up for a while. She sings, unaware of any danger, until the soaked cloth pulls her under. On stage you never see it happen. A queen only tells it.

Millais built the picture backward: scenery first, person last. In the summer of 1851 he sat on the bank of the Hogsmill, a small river in Surrey, south of London, for up to eleven hours a day, six days a week, about five months. He copied one stretch of bank leaf by leaf, leaving a blank in the middle of the canvas.

He wrote to a friend that the flies of Surrey were more muscular than any he had met, that the wind threatened to blow him into the water, and that he had been warned he could be summoned before a judge for trespassing in a field and flattening the hay.

Such stubbornness was a creed. Millais, himself only twenty-two, belonged to the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, a small band of young British painters who rejected the soft, brownish, flattering manner taught in art schools. Their rule: go outdoors and paint each thing exactly as it is. Even the things almost nobody will notice.
A small bird is watching the scene from the branches. Where?

spots.title: The robin
spots.text: A robin, red breast turned toward you, perched among the twigs on the far left. In her madness Ophelia sings a line about “bonny sweet Robin”.

lesson.text: You had to comb through a lot of twigs to get there, and every one is as sharp as the next. Nothing blurs with distance, which is not how eyes work, and it gives the scene its slightly feverish intensity. Millais also painted over a bright white ground, a white layer under the colors, so the greens glow like stained glass.

The plants are not only accurate. Victorians enjoyed a “language of flowers” in which each species carried a message, and Shakespeare names several in the play. Millais added some of his own. The stream can be read almost like a letter.

lesson.title: Four messages
lesson.text: Start with the brightest spot of color in the water.

spots.title: The poppy
spots.text: A red poppy with a dark heart, floating near her hand. Shakespeare does not mention one. Millais slipped it in: the poppy stands for sleep, and for death.

spots.title: Violets
spots.text: A chain of violets circles her neck. In the play Ophelia says the violets all withered when her father died. They spoke of faithfulness, and of dying young.

spots.title: Pansies
spots.text: Purple petals drift on the skirt. Ophelia hands out pansies earlier in the play: “that's for thoughts”. They could also mean love in vain.

spots.title: Dog roses
spots.text: Pale wild roses climb over the bank. Ophelia's brother calls her “rose of May”. A wild rose opens and drops within days: youth and beauty, briefly.

lesson.text: There was once an animal in the water too. Millais painted a water vole paddling beside Ophelia. When relatives saw the unfinished canvas, they guessed in turn that it was a hare, a rabbit, a dog and a cat. He scraped it out.

Shown at London's Royal Academy in 1852, the picture puzzled some critics, who thought a girl in a weedy ditch lacked dignity. The public never agreed. Siddal went on to paint and write poetry herself, married the painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and died at thirty-two from an overdose of laudanum, an opium-based medicine. It is hard to see her floating here without thinking of that.
The Pre-Raphaelites painted poetry with a botanist's eye: here every leaf is true to nature, and every flower means something.
You now know the picture was made in two halves, months apart: a summer riverbank and a winter bathtub. Wander through it on your own and see whether you can feel the seam.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Lips parted, eyes half open: she is still singing. This is Siddal, painted in the London studio months after the landscape was finished.

spots.title: Open hands
spots.text: Palms up, fingers loose. The gesture echoes saints and martyrs in older religious pictures, and lends a quiet holiness to her death.

spots.title: The dress
spots.text: An antique gown “all flowered over in silver embroidery”, as Millais described it. He bought it secondhand for four pounds. Air caught in the cloth keeps her afloat, for now.

spots.title: The willow
spots.text: The tree she was climbing when a branch gave way. A willow leaning over water was the emblem of forsaken love.

spots.title: Long purples
spots.text: Tall spikes of purple loosestrife. They are probably Millais's answer to the “long purples” that Shakespeare's queen lists among Ophelia's garlands.

spots.title: Forget-me-nots
spots.text: Tiny pale blue flowers on the far bank. Their name is the message.

spots.title: The reeds
spots.text: Stiff green blades painted one at a time on the bank in Surrey. Compare their hard edges with the softness of her skin, added indoors.

quiz.question: How did Elizabeth Siddal pose for Ophelia?
options: Lying in a bathtub of water in the studio
Lying on a studio floor covered with flowers
quiz.explanation: She lay dressed in a bath warmed by oil lamps, which one day went out.

quiz.question: In what order did Millais paint the picture?
options: The riverbank first, outdoors, then the figure in the studio
The figure first, then the landscape from memory
Everything at once, on the riverbank
quiz.explanation: He spent about five months on the landscape in 1851, then added Ophelia in winter.

quiz.question: What did the Pre-Raphaelites insist on?
options: Painting each thing exactly as it is in nature
quiz.explanation: They rejected art-school conventions and painted nature in sharp detail.

quiz.question: Which flower did Millais add even though Shakespeare never mentions it?
quiz.explanation: The red poppy, a symbol of sleep and death, is Millais's own addition.

quiz.question: Why did Millais remove the water vole?
options: Nobody who saw it could tell what animal it was
quiz.explanation: Relatives guessed hare, rabbit, dog and cat, so he scraped it out.

facts.text: Ophelia's drowning is acted out on stage in “Hamlet”.
facts.explanation: It happens offstage and is only described by the queen.

facts.text: A robin is hidden in the branches on the left of the painting.
facts.explanation: It may echo the “bonny sweet Robin” of Ophelia's song.

facts.text: Millais painted the riverbank from memory in his London studio.
facts.explanation: He painted it outdoors by the Hogsmill River, over about five months.
